content: 1. Treatment should be prioritized for individuals who are likely to gain the most significant personal benefit or for populations where treatment can substantially reduce hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission. 2. Those at the highest risk of mortality and morbidity include individuals at risk of accelerated liver fibrosis, those with metabolic syndrome, and those experiencing extrahepatic manifestations of HCV. 3. Populations where treatment could reduce the incidence of HCV include people who inject drugs (PWID), HIV-infected men who have sex with men (MSM), prisoners, sex workers, and healthcare workers. 4. Since the 2016 guidelines for HCV screening, care, and treatment, three major developments have influenced changes in treatment timing and choice: The widespread use of safe and highly effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens for all individuals has improved the benefit-to-harm ratio, supporting a strategy of treating all individuals with chronic HCV infection rather than reserving treatment for those with advanced disease. Before 2014, HCV treatment relied on interferon-based regimens, which had low cure rates, long treatment durations, and significant toxicities. The introduction of highly effective, well-tolerated, short-course oral DAA therapies, which achieve high sustained virological response (SVR) rates within weeks, has transformed the treatment landscape for chronic HCV infection. Several new pangenotypic DAA medications have been approved by stringent regulatory authorities, reducing the need for genotyping to guide treatment decisions. Examples include sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir, and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, which demonstrate high efficacy across all six major HCV genotypes, including in individuals with cirrhosis or HIV coinfection. 5. The continued substantial reduction in the cost of DAA regimens has enabled rapid treatment rollout in many lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). 6. Together, these factors have shifted the balance of benefits and risks in favor of treating all individuals with chronic HCV infection using pangenotypic regimens. 7. The primary audience for these guidelines includes policymakers in ministries of health in LMICs. The recommendations are intended to guide the development of national hepatitis policies, plans, and treatment guidelines. 8. For countries with existing national plans or programs, these guidelines can inform updates to national hepatitis treatment guidelines and decisions on which medicines to use. 9. Implementing partners can use these guidelines to design and implement treatment services, and clinicians treating HCV-infected individuals may also find them helpful. 10. The recommendations in these guidelines focus on treatment issues but also emphasize the importance of prevention, testing, and care as part of the continuum of care for HCV infection. 11. The management of acute HCV infection is not included in the scope of these guidelines. 12. These guidelines complement existing guidance on the primary prevention of HCV and other bloodborne viruses, including improving blood and injection safety and healthcare for people who inject drugs and other vulnerable groups, such as those living with HIV. 13. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that in 2015, 71 million people were living with chronic HCV infection globally, with a prevalence of 1%, and 399,000 deaths occurred due to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 14. HCV infection also contributes to an additional burden through comorbidities such as depression, diabetes mellitus, and chronic renal disease, some of which are directly attributable to HCV and are referred to as extrahepatic manifestations. 15. The World Health Assembly recognized viral hepatitis as a major public health problem and passed resolutions in 2010 and 2014 to address it. 16. In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) for 2016–2021 on viral hepatitis, aiming to eliminate it as a public health threat by 2030. Elimination is defined as a 90% reduction in new chronic infections and a 65% reduction in mortality compared to the 2015 baseline. 17. Achieving these targets requires diagnosing 90% of those infected and treating 80% of those diagnosed. However, in 2015, significant gaps remained, with only 7% of infected individuals started on treatment. 18. HCV infection can cause both acute and chronic hepatitis. Spontaneous clearance occurs in 15–45% of cases within six months, while 55–85% develop chronic infection, which can lead to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis. 19. The risk of cirrhosis ranges from 15% to 30% after 20 years of infection, and approximately 1–3% of individuals with cirrhosis progress to HCC annually. 20. Factors such as alcohol use, HBV or HIV coinfection, and immunosuppression increase the risk of cirrhosis and HCC. 21. HCV infection can lead to extrahepatic manifestations, with the most common comorbidities being depression (24%), diabetes mellitus (15%), and chronic renal disease (10%). 22. Coinfection with HIV accelerates the progression of HCV-related liver disease, particularly in individuals with advanced immunodeficiency. 23. In high-income countries, HCV-associated liver disease has become a leading cause of death among people living with HIV. 24. Unsafe healthcare practices, such as unsterilized injections and unscreened blood transfusions, contribute significantly to HCV transmission. 25. Injection drug use accounts for 23% of new HCV infections globally, and people who inject drugs are at increased risk of all-cause mortality due to combined factors such as low socioeconomic status and poor access to healthcare. 26. Sexual transmission of HCV is infrequent but more common among HIV-positive individuals, particularly men who have sex with men. 27. Pangenotypic DAA regimens, such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, achieve high efficacy across all HCV genotypes and are effective in various patient populations, including those with cirrhosis, renal insufficiency, or HIV coinfection. 28. The combination of sofosbuvir/daclatasvir has also demonstrated good efficacy in treating HCV infections across genotypes and is commonly used in LMICs. 29. The development and implementation of these guidelines are informed by principles such as promoting human rights, preventing stigma and discrimination, and ensuring gender equity in the provision of hepatitis services. 30. Local context, including HCV epidemiology, healthcare system capacity, and cost-effectiveness, should guide the implementation of these recommendations.
